utterances.text: More than once. I was taken out frequently and made to stand there the whole day. Then they would bring me in. They seemed to have some special sympathies for me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to Sanski Most. What did they ask you during that interview?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to go back, believe me. I don't know what they asked me. It's -- these are very difficult questions to which I am not sure I can give answers. I do recall some questions, but these questions were shocking to me. Believe me when I say that, because all of these people knew me well. They knew me well. Up until yesterday I was the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did they ask you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would ask me -- let's say Mr. Branko Sobot took me out one day and asked me about 20 automatic rifles. I was shocked. I froze up. What rifles? Please. I only said, "What are you doing to me, Branko? You know everything. Why are you asking me that?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you something about party -- the party arming itself? Did they ask you anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember questions like that being put. Mostly they had to do about me, certain charges against me. I practically had the impression at the time that I was already sentenced to death, and now it was up to me to defend myself. And this is specifically about me. There were no questions that had to do with the arming or politics or policies. I had a question, for example that, there were trenches found around my home. Or that, after my arrest, heavy weaponry was found in my home, for example. Or that I preferred in court to deal with cases of Muslims, Bosniaks, rather than Serbs. These questions were really shocking to me, and I saw where all of this was leading, and I knew that the death sentence is unavoidable in my case. And I'm really telling you, at no point was I asked about arming, because all I could have said that there was no arming at all, especially not in the Mahala. I know that there was no arming in the Mahala because that's where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please turn to the second page of this document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also look at the next page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but this document that you gave me deserves attention. This is also a statement that was given in prison. It's a statement by Mr. Sabic Suad. I don't know if it's a complete statement or not. This is something that only Mr. Sabic can talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand you, absolutely, Mr. Draganovic. Can you please turn the page and you can see at the top, on the third line marked by the number 20 by hand, and then underneath the photograph we can see the number 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then we can scroll up, scroll up. Scroll down. Scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you see in Sarajevo when there was a referendum about the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you travel to Sarajevo with Sabic and the others? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes. That is correct from that report that we travelled together, because I was supposed to hand over the referendum material because I was the president of the referendum commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. We need to go faster. I do understand. Please, I just need short answers, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And these individuals that are listed there travelled with you. Some of them travelled in police vehicles. That was you, and Buric Enver who was the police station commander, and then Ismet Sarcevic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the -- in the other vehicle -- the other vehicle contained these other individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Ismet Sarcevic, and now, that's under 22, item 22, actually established contact with our people? I assume that this "our people" refers to SDS people in Visoko and that they resumed with arming people there. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Now, tell me this: On page 3 of this document, that is the statement of Mr. Sabic continues there, and he speaks about -- and that's under item 33 and then 38A and 39, he speaks about the position of the Main Staff of the SDA in Sarajevo were to actually drag out the negotiations about the three coalition parties. And also, as we can see under 38A, there was a rift within the police station in Sanski Most and in the Territorial Defence so that the SDA then decided that they would establish their own organs and police in the NTO in the municipality. Would you agree with what is stated there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't agree with this part, because I can tell you about the rift. What I can tell you is that this man was arrested at the same time that I was arrested, and I can really not speak about how and where he was interviewed, but I could not agree with this position of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with what he states under number 40, where he says that all police officers or -- or, rather, all employees of the police of Muslim or Croat ethnicity who did not remain in the Serbian part of the police, that they were invited by the SDA to establish a Muslim police station? Do you agree with the words and the statement of Mr. Sabic there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you this: I did not take part in the work of the party, and I don't know what the party position was, but I can just briefly comment on what had led to the rift in the police. The policemen of Muslim nationality or Muslim ethnicity were expelled from the police station, and I'm sure there were testimonies to that effect, and evidence as well, and documents. So people just left, or they went to the Sanski Most municipality after consulting the SDA officials and had a meeting there. They barricaded themselves in there, and probably they had that intention. On the 17th of that month -- what month was that? I believe that was April, in April 1992. They had to leave that building, and they just disappeared. Practically they left the building under duress because some shells were fired at them from a -- from an APC. The shells were fired at the building. They threatened that they would destroy the -- pull down the municipal building, so they left the building on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know of any political arrangements about the division within Sanski Most municipality. Was there any mention of such things?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were a lot of things being discussed. Certainly there were people negotiating, because people wanted to avoid armed conflict. And the SDA officials had the very best intention. They offered, if necessary, to divide the territory of Sanski Most municipality, and in that sense such things were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to know. Now, tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, for, I suppose the nth time, we've got Mr. Trbojevic waiting. It's the second time he's back. He's not very happy altogether, but can I ask whether -- how long Mr. Pantelic is going to be now and whether Mr. Cvijetic, who is not really -- whose client is not affected by this witness at all, has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, before Mr. Pantelic answers the question about time, would I bring to his attention that at this point you would have spent two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the information. I must say not more than ten minutes, maybe 11, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Ms. Korner, it would appear that we would to get your witness today --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't know that -- I'm hoping that Mr. Cvijetic has no questions, but I don't imagine that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I have some questions, and I need at least one session to question this witness, and I believe that I will probably also need a part of the next session. And if Ms. Korner is asking because of the next witness, I believe that the next witness can only be brought in tomorrow, because the questioning by Mr. Pantelic and the replies provided by this witness actually broach certain topics that are relevant to Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm sorry, we're going to object to this now. We are -- we've asked over and over again for realistic estimates of time. We have at the moment, therefore, two witnesses waiting to give evidence on the basis that this witness would be concluded in at least halfway through the second session today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we requested two hours, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is our information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The request may be so, but, Your Honour, this witness was one hour in chief. Your general ruling was that the Defence would get roughly the same time to cross-examine. Now, I certainly appreciate that this witness is relevant to the case of Mr. Zupljanin. I do not see in what conceivable way this witness can be relevant to the case of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I must object. I must object, Your Honour. Approach 92 ter is absolutely unbearable for the Defence, so, you know, it's very easy for the Prosecution to say one hour, let's say, and let's have thousands of transcript pages and documents. So we are in that situation, Your Honour. Please understand our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, the -- Mr. Pantelic may have expressed the observation I was about to make in a more agitated manner than I would have chosen, but the point is that with 92 ter witnesses, in terms of time, clearly the time is the -- the sharing of time favours the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that. Well, all I can say is that if Mr. Cvijetic insists on cross-examining for more than one session, then we're -- we're backing up all over again with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, we rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, just to wrap up this part of questioning, the magazine or the newspaper "Walter" that we see before us on the screens, this is a federation newspaper; is that correct? The Muslim-Croat federation.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is published in Sarajevo, and of course I don't know how many readers it has and who buys it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document. Can I get the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I object to it -- or I don't think it was -- an application wasn't made to tender it last time because the witness didn't know anything about it. So it just stayed in abeyance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is new witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm not objecting, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit 2D28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I forget the date of the article. Could you refresh my mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's 15 May 2001, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, could you agree with me that the part relating to the pre-trial proceedings and the investigating phase of a trial contains such activities as information interviews? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these information interviews can be characterised as the pre-trial phase of a proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So when a public prosecutor in -- at a certain stage, or the investigating judge at the next stage, assesses that it is necessary to complete this procedure with some additional statements and information, then they issue or instruct the police to conduct an interview to collect information; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the -- the very fact that a statement is produced -- and this phase of the investigation is actually initiated by the prosecutor, because the police is not authorised to take any action without instructions from the prosecutor, except in emergency situations where it concerns detection of crimes and apprehension of perpetrators. We can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, and what I'm putting to you is that on the basis of what you said, you have provided a number of such statements both in Manjaca and to the police, which means that there was -- that some procedure was initiated against you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. There were no criminal proceedings initiated against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well -- but if you say that your statements were provided as part of these interviews to collect information, then there must have been some kind of prosecution initiated, I assume before military organs.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not -- I was not interviewed by military organs in Sanski Most. I was interviewed, and I made these statements which were not written, nor did I sign anything in Sanski Most, but I provided these statements to the police. I was interviewed by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Manjaca, I was taken out for questioning by military policemen, and I assume that I was questioned by some kind of military investigator, because I saw that this person was wearing a uniform. But who this person was, whether he was a military person or a security man, I don't know, because I had never seen the man before, nor did I ever see him after that. But I have to say that he was quite -- he treated me quite fairly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, you're an experienced judge, and you spent many years working as an investigating judge as well. Once -- so tell us, once an order is issued to the police to conduct an interview to collect information or to prepare an official note regarding a certain event, this then initiates proceedings, and there are no limits, really. This can go on up until the moment when the crime itself actually enjoys the statute of limitations; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking questions that I can't really answer. I have to react to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, please allow me --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you, but I have to interfere here, intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you to answer me. If there is a certain investigating procedure initiated and if a statement is taken from a person, there is no limit to this. This can go on for as long as an investigation is ongoing; correct? There is no other limitation except when the crime actually expires.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to reply. It's not a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, please answer my question. As the president and investigating judge, please tell me -- I'm just asking you to comment the legal provisions. So I'm asking you, an informative -- information interview is conducted based on an order from an investigating judge or from a prosecutor; correct? But there is one -- one proceeding is instituted; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in a cell for 44 days. I never -- I was never issued any written statement regarding my detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, please answer my questions. I'm asking you as the president of the court, a professional, an attorney, an investigating judge. If there is a -- if criminal proceedings have been instituted, there may be one, two, five, ten, or a hundred interviews conducted with the accused; correct? Or the suspect; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The interview can be carried out, but you're limited as to the time, for how long I can be in detention. There must be a request by the prosecutor. If there is no request by the prosecutor you have to release me. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you now and I'm asking you, what was the deadline for detention according to the law from 1992? How long could a state be -- a person be held in detention for a maximum period?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, there was a maximum period of time for up to three days. This is police custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what about the prosecutor's custody?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor's custody is for a period of one month. It can be extended after that, but the person must have an attorney and must have everyone -- everything according to regulations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat his answer because the Defence attorney and the witness are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You're overlapping. The interpreters are having difficulty keeping up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the -- Mr. Draganovic, the -- Mr. Draganovic, I'm sorry, the interpreters need you to repeat the answer, your last answer. Perhaps Mr. Pantelic could assist with repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Draganovic, it's a short and clear question. According to the criminal law of 1992 that was in force then, how long could judicial detention last for a maximum period of time? Let me help you there a little bit. You had the Trial Chamber, the right of appeal. So what was the maximum period of time that it could last?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you now -- all right, just wait. I'm speaking now. You can speak later with the Prosecutor, but what I'm telling you now is this: There was a requisite procedure conducted against you before the investigative organs in Manjaca and because of the -- and before the military court in Banja Luka for illegal actions and for possession of weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm hearing this, and it's good that you told me that so that I know. I never heard that before, nor was I ever informed, nor did I ever receive a single document in which what you are saying now was stated, and if I had received that, then I would have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: In 1995, when you came to Sanski Most, how long -- how many members of the Serb ethnicity were in Sanski Most? If you have the number, you can please tell me. If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serbs there are in Sanski Most right now?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned that 18.000 non-Serbs left from Sanski Most, on what basis did you state that piece of information? Do you have any evidence of that? Is there some sort of calculation that you were able to do?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just tell me where this evidence can be found.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This evidence can be found in reports of the Serbian Assembly or the Executive Board of the Serbian Assembly of the municipality of Sanski Most, because they looked at the numbers at their meeting in 1992. They monitored the numbers of non-Serbs who were still living in the territory of the Sanski Most municipality. And that's there. I also know on the basis of some data that I established after the war. This is information by the International Red Cross and other information that I researched from statements by witnesses and certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Draganovic, but you're not a demographics expert, so you can't really help us much in that area.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. In 1995, when you came and then when you initiated investigations, you mentioned that you found in the vault of the Police Chief Vrucinic a green folder with some documents in it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did give that statement in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This file was found with documents.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. There were several files actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you personally keep any of those documents for your own purposes perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I kept any of the documents for my own purposes, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you hand over the entire documentation to the Secret Service, the AID, then or later?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed over a part of some of that documentation to the AID, the Agency for Investigations and Protection. I handed over some of the documents to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. There are about 4.000 documents here that I handed over. These documents were taken from Sanski Most, and they were listed in an official record. The investigator Ms. or Mrs. Paczulla, I think that was her name, from Canada. And the rest of the documents were handed over to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But there were copies of all the documents, so there was a trail of where each document went so that all relevant organs were informed about the documents, and the originals were kept at a certain location until they were officially handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you sign those receipts and certificates about the hand-over the documents?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I did sign some reports about submission of documents, sending out of documents. The ones that I handed over I signed for, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you don't have anything in your own possession of those documents from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than some copies, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What copies?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that diary and maybe some other documents which were -- well, these were perhaps some decisions by the Crisis Staff regarding my arrest -- or at the time of my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you don't have the originals?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have the originals now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that representative of the Tribunal, was her name Jutta Paczulla?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's spelled P-a-c-z-u-l-l-a. I think Your Honours may have seen that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell me, Mr. Draganovic, since you testified quite a lot before this Tribunal and the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, since 1995, how frequently did you have contact with the AID Secret Service? How many times did you have conversations with them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I was an investigating judge and the president of the court. When I needed to check certain things or to get some information, I would then call those people to service me in that aspect and to assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During your preparations for your testimony, you had meetings with AID representatives regarding the circumstances about which you would certify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, and you can be sure that I did not have any contacts or talks for the purposes of any testimony that I gave. As I said, I just used those certain people that were handy to help me about matters that I was investigating as an investigating judge, in order to gather certain information, knowledge, so on. I did not submit any reports to the AID. I used them as a service to help me in my work as an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But, my colleague, Mr. Draganovic, I think that you exaggerated when testifying and responding to answers by my learned friend Mr. Di Fazio here. I think that you exaggerated with your assessment. It was sort of literal for purposes of creating a certain effect. How can you compare Manjaca and describe it as a death camp? Isn't that a little excessive? Let me just tell you one thing, Mr. Draganovic. I myself, as your colleague, do not dispute in any way that you had very, very distressing experiences, and let us hope something like that is never repeated. That is my opinion. But I really believe that you're adding salt to the wound here. How could you say for Manjaca that it was a death camp, that people were killed there, burned there? Was that set up so that people would be destroyed? Please, Mr. Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I respect you as a colleague, and I respect and appreciate the work that you are doing. At no point was I was a poet here. I was really testifying about what I think and what I experienced. The time doesn't permit for me now to talk to you about that, you understand. You would all have goose bumps. You have my testimony. I stand by it, I believe that it was clear, and I swear by my all that the first two or three months, it was a death camp. And the conditions in which we were staying there, I simply did not believe that I would survive them. None of us believed that we would survive that: Beatings, mistreatment, lack of food, conditions that were in -- what else was that than an attempt to destroy all of us who were there? And you can be sure I would not wish something like that upon anyone. That is all. You have everything in my testimony, and I stand by my words that it was precisely like that, and I'm sure all the inmates who passed through Manjaca would say the same thing. That is why I said initially it was like that. Later, the conditions were more bearable. But the way a man felt was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Draganovic. Let us finish this question. I would just like to say one thing to you. I personally cannot understand. As I said, there were incidents there, and ultimately people were brought to trial because of that in Banja Luka, but what I'm saying is that it is impossible that Manjaca was a death camp, because in that case you would have mass killings there, executions. I understand a death camp to be something that the Nazis committed to people they conquered in World War II. You cannot make that parallel in that way. That is a death camp. This is what I wanted to say. I think that you are exaggerating. I think it would be fair for you to qualify your assessment, to tone down your assessment.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to say that this was not the same as the Omarska camp, that the conditions there were much worse. People were getting killed there en masse in Omarska, and Keraterm in Prijedor. Here we didn't have physical liquidations in the same numbers as -- or in proportion to the number of people who were being detained there. But a death camp -- look, at that time, during the first two or three months, the way it was, had it continued that way, we would all have died or have been killed. None of us would have remained alive. Let me just give you one example. Two days ago I was speaking to my wife who said, "Ilijaz, Professor Ilijaz Avdic, inmate, died." He was an inmate together with me. There is no day that passes without somebody dying. Professor Ilijaz Pasic is 54 years old. Last year Dr. Mehmed Derviskadic died, who treated all of us inmates. And he was only 50 years old. I said that more than 500 people have died. Not a single day passes without a person dying in Bosnia-Herzegovina of the people who had been in Manjaca. They could be abroad as well. It doesn't matter. This is why I'm saying that this is a death camp because it has caused so much death and suffering for all the people who passed through that camp. During the time that the camp was operating, 5 to 6.000 people passed through that camp. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Really, with all due respect to those who were victims who died, but, please, are you a medical expert? How do you know what the reason is for all of that? How can you talk about that as well? Just tell me, are you a medical expert or not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I begin, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Draganovic, good day.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I am Slobodan Cvijetic. I'm in the Defence team of Mr. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that you returned to Sanski Most on the 15th of October, 1995. You said that in the Brdjanin case, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So this is an accurate fact.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Not right away, but you began to carry out investigations - that's what you said - about possible war crimes which occurred in the Sanski Most municipality during 1992. And later, I assume. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I got the impression that you didn't form an official formal body or a commission that would deal with these matters. I think that you responded to one question that you had received a verbal suggestion from the Sanski Most War Presidency to begin such work. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a written note from the Sanski Most War Presidency, but I also worked pursuant to the authority of the Cantonal Court and the cantonal prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I would like to know if you have those written documents.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those documents exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you show them to the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think those documents do exist. I don't recall whether I showed them to anyone or not. These are just investigative actions pursuant to the criminal law. I was authorised to do that. I don't remember if I provided those documents to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And those investigating activities also involved research into the mass graves that were discovered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And these are precisely the investigations that I carried out pursuant to instructions or the authority issued by the president of the Bihac Cantonal Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When I put a question to you, just make a short break. We have already been warned not to overlap. However, in your statement you said that on return from such an investigation, you frequently of your own initiative would stop by at Mr. Rasula's house or to the apartment of the representative of the national security service. I don't remember his name right now. And in that way, you would look for documents which you would consider to be relevant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not completely correct, the way you formulated your question. What I can say is that on those first days when I came back, I had an assignment, and I also base this on my discussion with the Prosecutor, that I should establish the locations where I could find some documents about the war crimes. Now, I was informed -- I had been informed that Mr. Nedeljko Rasula's house in Caplje [phoen] village had already been occupied by someone. A man of Bosniak ethnicity had moved into his house, and so I gained entry into that house with a number of witnesses, because this man was already living there, and I obtained those documents. I got them there in that house. This was in keeping or in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, and I gained entry legally and lawfully and seized those documents. They would have been burned, probably, because many of those documents had already been thrown out as garbage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So at the moment when you actually entered the house, you did not actually have a legal document that would allow you to do so?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as an investigating judge, I didn't need any such -- any such formal document other than the approval of the prosecutor, and I had obtained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What kind of approval did you obtain from the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a conversation over the phone, so the approval of the prosecutor could be either before the fact or after the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this is the manner in which you then proceeded to obtain the documents that we've seen here before us?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1995, when Sanski Most was captured or, as you would say, liberated by the BH Army, Serbian civilians left Sanski Most in large numbers, and some of the buildings that were the property of Serbs were destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There were also a number of killings of Serb civilians; correct? And in the case -- in the Brdjanin case, there was a list of such civilians put to you. Now, if I can ask you, then, did you make any progress regarding this document, because at that time you were not willing to comment it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you remind me what I said then about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, looking at the list, you said - and you weren't even sure of that - that you had only conducted one investigation regarding one man who had been killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really can't remember, because during the proofing session I did not have occasion to read through this list again, and if I was shown -- and to read through my statement, my earlier testimony. Now, if I was shown a statement and I said that, that's probably true. And I probably conducted investigations --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do we have a transcript notation for this, for this testimony? It would make it easier for the Prosecution and all the parties to follow the evidence if we could get the transcript from the Brdjanin case where this -- this material was put. A page number, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am putting this to the witness directly and asking him if he can recall this fact. I don't want to go back and revisit the entire Brdjanin case. I'm just asking the witness whether he remembers this fact whether he had conducted any investigation into the death of that civilian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I stated, and I stay by what I said then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And what is your answer to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer is the same, but do put my answer to me, please. Remind me of what I said. I can't recall it now, because a lot of time has passed. I haven't seen the document since, and I can't really recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, and here's the list --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's precisely the problem I was talking about, and that's why we need the transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a list of dead individuals in hard copy, and only -- all I can do is perhaps put this list to the witness, ask him if he remembers it, and then perhaps he can give us his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've been through this with Mr. Cvijetic over and over again. If he wants to say that the witness said something in the previous trial, he must come armed with a copy of the transcript, a copy of the answer, and the page number. I know he can't read English and therefore he has to listen to the tape, but if there's something he wants to put to the witness, then he must be able to sort it out with one of his team who speaks English as to what the page number is. I hope Mr. Cvijetic understand that. The witness is now asked to have his answer put to him. If he can't put the answer to him, then he cannot continue with this line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may assist, Mr. Cvijetic. The distinction which apparently the -- is being lost and the point that Ms. Korner is making is that there is a distinction between what you understand the facts to be and putting to the witness what he said on a previous occasion; and if you are, in fact, seeking to do the latter, then, as Ms. Korner said, you have to be in a position to put what he said, not rely on what you understand the background facts to be. So that's the distinction that is necessary for you to keep in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have that, Your Honour. This is the transcript of the 22nd of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm trying to help the witness by showing him the list of individuals. This was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 22nd of May of what year, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2002. I apologise. I made an error. I said 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman asked you whether you had conducted an investigation into the death of this individual, and then he showed you this document. And what I would like to do now is show you that same list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please assist me. So this was put to the witness during the cross-examination conducted by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness asked you, "What was my answer?" You now said what Mr. Ackerman asked him. What was his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, not all of it. Just the last page. Could you please give me the document back so I can find that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all the documents, just this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I know Mr. Di Fazio is taking the witness, but this is really important. It hasn't still sunk into Mr. Cvijetic. He must have in front of him the transcript in English and read out in English the answer that Mr. Draganovic gave to Mr. Ackerman, not show him the document. And we would like the page number of the transcript on which this answer is said to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If I can get the page number it will solve a lot of things and then I will be able to follow the evidence. It's just the page number that would assist. I've got the transcript here and I've got the 22nd out, but I just don't have -- and I've got Mr. Ackerman's portion of that transcript. I still just need that little extra bit of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was on the 23rd of May, 2002. The question was: "After the Serbs left, did you assist in conducting an investigation into the killings of these individuals, the list of which I'm going to show you?" And I will -- I promise that I will have the exact page number and everything tomorrow morning when we continue with this witness, but I'm just asking this witness, when he was answering this question, the question was did he conduct an investigation into the killing of this Serbs. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did conduct ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, when you have the page number, then you can put the question to the witness. At this point, no -- this simply isn't going to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honours. So I will leave this aside for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Draganovic, my question was specific. Did you conduct any investigations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did conduct investigations -- or, rather, certain procedures in these investigations, and I would like to point out that there is a difference between an investigation and investigative procedures. So when I was -- when I received information from the police that a body was found, then would I conduct an on-site investigation. I would put together a team and we would go to the site, the crime site, and find -- and conduct an investigation. I would do that when informed, when such a body was found and reported to me. If not, I couldn't go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us how many such investigations you conducted?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to actually recall that. It's hard to specify anything without a detailed analysis, because after all, there is no indication when you find a body whether that body belonged to a Muslim, Serb, or Croat. You will agree with me that it's impossible to determine the identity of a person, and especially so as some of those bodies were in a very advanced state of decomposition. Sometimes we would even just find bones and clothes on them. They would be a couple of years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, this -- the documents that you found, you mentioned in respect of those documents that you co-operated with the investigation and information agency; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was an agency for investigations and protection. Their task was to investigate crimes. I've already testified about this in the Brdjanin case, and also during my evidence here I mentioned that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, we have that batch of documents here with us. I will try to classify them in groups of documents, and I would appreciate it if you could help me with that classification, because there are over 100 documents in there. Some of the documents, the only -- there are some documents that you said you only knew about because you had found them, but you didn't know anything about the content itself. You said that there were some orders there from the police or military that you wouldn't even have known about because -- you couldn't have known about because at the time you were in detention; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For another group of documents you said that you had read them and then drawn certain conclusions based on them. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I cannot really answer your question, because without a specific document being put to me and my opinion or conclusion that I offered at the time being put to me, I cannot really confirm whether that was so or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I will put a very specific example to you. For instance, on the 19th of April, 1992, there was a meeting attended by representatives of the army, the representatives of the SDA, the SDS, and the purpose of the meeting was to try and overcome the problems that were then in evidence in Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the first part of the question? I didn't get it quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a meeting. There was an attempt at the time. There was a meeting held at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you learned about what went on in that meeting by reading the relevant portions relating to that meeting in the entries or in the diary by Mr. Rasula; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I learned about what went on in that meeting already on the same day or the next day after the meeting, but I also confirmed some of the knowledge by reading through the diary. But I learned from some of the people who had attended the meeting about the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. But you did not attend it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was on the premises at the time. I was in the municipal building. I could see that the hall where the meeting was held was guarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, where are we going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm leading to the fact that there were numerous conclusions made by this witness, both in the Brdjanin case and here, that are second-hand facts, as it were. They are not first-hand information. And I also want to put to him some other statements that he made that weren't direct knowledge of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I suggest that you confront the witness exactly with the facts that you wish him to confirm or to deny rather than having to go through all his previous statements to see if there's any inconsistencies in the -- in the possible explanations that he has given to this. I mean, go for it head on. By that approach we might save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is my purpose, Your Honour. I am going to be direct now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we've already concluded that you did not attend this very important meeting.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've heard your answer. So you did not attend it. You then said that in many cases concerning various events you actually put it together or reconstructed the events, as it were, later on because you were in Manjaca at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again I have to say that I cannot actually give you an affirmative answer to this, because the knowledge that I had was derived from various documents, but also some information actually came through to me even while I was in Manjaca, in the camp, or at the time when these events were actually occurring. And there was also knowledge that I obtained after interviews with witnesses who actually participated in the events. So that is why I have to answer your question in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, to be specific, could you please tell us specifically what is your knowledge? How many victims were there actually in Manjaca camp? How many people died there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know, myself, of the victims that were in the vicinity of the camp and in the camp itself. For instance, Muhamed Filipovic was killed in the camp. There was a boy whose name was Bender who died there. Then there was a young man, Esad Delalovic, a policeman from Sanski Most, Emir -- I forget his last name. So as far as I can recall now, these were the people who were killed in the camp itself. There was also a member of the HOS who was killed there, but I don't know of this. We didn't see this killing. We could only hear it. He was killed in the stable. We could only see when he was taken to the stable, and we heard shots. But, for instance, there were these eight instances where people were killed, people who had been brought from Omarska camp. And on the morning when these people were supposed to come to -- or enter the camp itself they were killed, and I could see this myself. Later on I learnt -- or, rather, I learned -- while I was still at the camp I learned from Dr. Derviskadic, on that same evening, that 24 men from Sanski Most, from Sanski Most, had been killed while they were transported from Manjaca -- from Sanski Most to Manjaca. They had suffocated. I learned of that that same evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, please. I -- my question was: What is your certain knowledge? How many men were killed in Manjaca itself, or died in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my assessment is that about 60 people died there. I cannot really confirm and claim with certainty whether this is correct or not, but after I analysed the numbers and the cases that I had learned about and that I also saw myself, and also taking into account a number of bodies that had been thrown into a pit, bodies that had been brought there from Kljuc, and I only learned about it later on. They were found in the vicinity of Manjaca. So based on all this information, I assessed that about 60 people were killed, or maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Draganovic, that is taking into account the men who had suffocated and those who you heard of later on and so on, but directly in Manjaca, how many men do you know were killed there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, eight plus four plus one directly. That's my direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. So it is the number that I mentioned to you, 12 plus 1; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I apologise to the victims if I omitted anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now -- Manjaca was visited by Lord Ashdown; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Paddy Ashdown came to the camp. Of course, at the time I didn't know who the gentleman was or what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Manjaca was also visited by members of a Muslim charity, Merhamet; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they came from Banja Luka. They visited the camp once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Members of the International Red Cross also came, as well as journalists; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, you do not agree with the statement by Mr. Ashdown or the reports of the charity Merhamet, the Muslim charity, when they speak about the situation in Manjaca camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was only one statement of Mr. Ashdown's that I did not agree with. I agreed with everything else he said, but there was one thing where I actually did not agree with what he said, and that is when he mentioned that there was -- or, rather, that life in the camp had the semblance of order and organisation. So that is the aspect I could not agree with. I agreed with everything else. This was an interview conducted by a BBC journalist with Mr. Ashdown. As for the report by Merhamet, I did not agree with that report because I don't think it was given in the way that I gave it, because those people were under observation and monitoring, and they were unable -- probably wouldn't have been able to come had it had not been so. But the fact that they came meant a lot to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. So specifically, did Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki also come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he did come to the camp on one occasion, Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki. He did come to the Manjaca camp, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did he enter the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, from what I can recall, but this was late at night, perhaps around midnight. I don't know why, but around midnight when there were no lights or nothing, he couldn't see anything except us like monsters being held in those stables.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the meantime I have received from the service relating to Mr. Ackerman's service, this is page 5952, line 8. Mr. Di Fazio asked for a specific, and that reference is there for my question. However, I'm going to show that exactly to the witness tomorrow. I'm going to show and would ask to have the witness, please, shown a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, if it is correct that eight -- or, rather, 14 people died in the camp, you would agree with me that on the basis of the total number of persons who were there, the conclusion cannot be drawn that it was, in fact, a death camp, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my position.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There's a lot of background noise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of persons were taken from the Manjaca camp to the Kljuc municipality area where some ten people were killed there. Then a number of persons were taken to the Batkovic camp, about 500 of them, when this camp was disbanded, and at least two people were killed there. So that it is hard to say. I don't know what happened to people who were taken out of the camp who were from the Kotor Varos municipality, specifically from the Vecici village, who were also captured in forests and who spent a certain period of time in the camp. I don't know what happened to them afterwards. Some groups were also taken for exchange to the military investigative gaol in Banja Luka, to a small camp, Mali Logor. I cannot know the exact number of those who died of the people who passed through that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please show one document to the witness that is on the 65 ter list, 3037.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, do you see this document? And in the top left-hand corner you can see who it's by.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the first page of that document. I don't see the rest. And I can see that it's the 1st Krajina Corps Command, and I see that the date is the 23rd of August, 1992. I can also see that it's a strictly confidential document, number 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the title of the document, Mr. Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title of the document is: "The visit by UN representative Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki," and it's a report to the Government of Republika Srpska, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the forward command post of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 2 of this document now, please. Can you look at the last paragraph there, please.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that the document was signed by the assistant commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, no. Look at the last paragraph of the text.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. "Regardless of the consequences of the cancellation of Mr. Mazowiecki's visit to the prisoner-of-war camp, we declare with full responsibility that the purpose of his visit was not inspecting of the state of the human rights, but on the contrary, intelligence, reconnaissance which can be confirmed by those requesting the government of the AR," and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I concluded on this document and from other documents that you can see that the visit to -- by Mr. Mazowiecki was cancelled or forbidden and that he did not enter the camp.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you see that, then I correct my statement. And this is possible, because I couldn't have known, believe me. I know that many groups did come, but I did not prepare myself to know whether he was there or not. I know that there was quite a fiery debate about that, and I think that he submitted his irreversible resignation to his duties at the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, the essence of my question is consistent with the suggestion by His Honour Judge Harhoff to submit evidence on the basis of which we can conclude that you sometimes draw conclusions indirectly. In response to my question, you categorically stated that Tadeusz Mazowiecki did visit the camp, but now you're withdrawing that part your statement after I've showed you this document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but my learned friend, you are behaving a little bit sneakily. I guess that is part of your job. I said that there were many international representatives, and I have already said that I didn't know Mr. Ashdown, what his name was when he was up there, but I, of course, found that out later. But I did know that Mr. Elie Wiesel was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, I didn't ask about Mr. Elie Wiesel. All right. Just -- just be patient.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment. I apologise, but one more time. It's possible that I made --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: A mistake here.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Was brought into a confusing situation, and I accept that it is possible that Mr. Mazowiecki did not enter, was not in the camp, because you must know how much time has passed and that my recollection and memory is beginning to pale slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's my question. I'm not taking that against you, but I would like you to answer me sincerely. Is it true that many information -- much information on which you testified about was information you acquired indirectly, without personal knowledge of the relevant facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just answer me with a yes or no. Well, I will be happy --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer with a yes or no. I am responding to your question by saying that I already spoke about that when I testified in the Brdjanin and Galic cases, how and in what way I acquired information and I am repeating that position and response of mine right now. These are several ways in which I got that information and from several sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. How did you find out that the civilian police - specifically you said from Kljuc - was entering the camp and was mistreating the inmates there? Did you personally observe any such incident? Briefly, if you can.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My cousins, or my relatives, whose last name is also Draganovic, are from Kljuc. I'm also from Kljuc. And my information comes from them, that these were policemen from Kljuc whom they personally know. I didn't know those people personally. So I could see it that those people were beaten up. They were lying there beaten up every night. We were concerned that they would be called out. I was most afraid also that I would also be called out also because my last name was Draganovic, that we shared the same last name, that I'm also born in Kljuc. But thank God, they did not call me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right I'm satisfied with the answer. You said you didn't personally see that abuse. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment. All of those things, when we're talking about mistreatment and the beatings, not only did I find out about that from the stories of those who actually experienced that, I heard that with my own ears. Do you understand? And I saw some beatings. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping. It's very difficult for the interpreters to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, Counsel and Witness, the interpreters are having a difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We mustn't overlap. You must wait for me to interrupt you at least. Mr. Draganovic, Mr. Draganovic, when you -- did you say anything about the arrival or coming in of the police from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: To Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk about that in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And how did they behave?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to hear that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the police from Sanski Most behaved more correctly than the police from Kljuc because they did not take people out. They did not participate in the beatings of people. And I think that is quite clear what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us continue. You also testified about the death of --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment. I do remember one thing. One police officer, reserve police officer, only one, beat up one of his professors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. You talked about the death of Mr. Omer Filipovic also; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I notice it's almost time and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's time, but perhaps may I just ask for one indulgence and that's this: A few minutes ago counsel for the Defence referred to a document involved -- concerning the visit of Mazowiecki, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, to the area, and that document was 65 ter 3037. It should -- it should be exhibited or at the very least marked for identification. The Prosecution application is to admit it fully into evidence, unless, of course, the Defence want to tender it into evidence fully, in which case the Prosecution would have no objection to that course of action. But, one way or another, it should go into evidence. And if not, if you're not with me on that, it should be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Cvijetic, what is your position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how much the witness knows about this document, but I can propose it for admission. That is not something that the Defence would be against, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain why. Witnesses will come who know about this document directly, and I tried to avoid criticism in that sense, but if the Prosecutor would like to have it admitted, I tender it, then. I'm not opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention one other matter in relation to Mr. Cvijetic's cross-examination and that's this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 1D87, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's just this: It's the matter I raised earlier on. Everything he's asking about is actually covered in the nine days that Mr. Draganovic testified in the Brdjanin case, which I'm afraid to say I take some responsibility; but nonetheless, we are literally rehashing this, as he keeps saying what is in the transcript, and I'm just wondering whether Your Honours might suggest to Mr. Cvijetic that repeating what's already in evidence, through the transcript, is not very productive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, he will have overnight to reflect on your observation, your helpful observation, Mrs. Korner. Thank you. We resume in this Chamber tomorrow morning at 9.00. And, Mr. Draganovic, I am obliged to repeat the usual warning about not contacting or not speak with the lawyers or discussing your testimony with anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 2nd day of December, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
